comments.author: RichardTheApe
comments.body:
I could be bias as my wheel house is typically strategy/simulation games but I’d actually push the time:complexity axis higher. 

I agree that AI efficiency pushes it much higher, probably more for my genre given the data heavy nature of it but I’d say a small game still takes reliably closer to a year with true AI gold firmly in the TBD/1+ year mark. 

This isn’t to be a doomer, just that I think the first part of good dev is realistic goals and standards. Anyone seriously considering building their dream game needs to budget realistically. We’ve already just become spoiled by AI in the best way possible because for reference 

Stardew valley was in development for 4 years of active development before it even came to steam as an alpha 

Lethal company, 2 years before alpha

Vampire survivors, the simplest(by some measurements) took just over a year before alpha. 

Just all to say while we are entering a production renaissance we ought to as always remain focused on realistic expectations as they exist for us. All to say that maybe in a year I’ll be eating my own words but I happily invite to be proven wrong in this circumstance.

comments.author: NBMVegeta
comments.body:
I can somewhat agree and relate to the shared graph with my own experience even without using frontier models. I used Google AI Studio to make a AI slop Quality Play store clone to test out how much time it takes and what it makes with few prompts. 
Day 1 - It created the foundational level core with basic gameplay of course with issues, but otherwise it would have taken a Game Developer with few months of time. 
Day 30 - I am still trying to fix and improve logics here and there but released the game to play store. 
Did this as a side project with a full time job.
After Gemini 3.8 Flash release, again tried to check the quality and improvements of new model so used AI Studio and I selected it's auto-fill prompts and just 1 prompt gave an amazing output.
